utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I assume that the JNA tanks had Yugoslav flags on them, whereas the soldiers could have Serbian flags with them. That's what you're saying. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could clarify something.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Karlovic, when you say "flags," are you referring to normal-sized flags or small flags sewn onto to the clothes of the men? I'm referring to the flags that were borne by these various individuals?

utterances.speaker: VILLEM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am thinking of a flag that is unfolded and also the markings that are on the uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I understand. To be more specific, the Territorial Defence had flags, perhaps on their uniforms, and these flags represented what exactly? Was it a Yugoslav army flag? Was it a Serbian flag? Could you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: VILLEM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Witness, I'll put a question to you. Perhaps you won't be able to answer it because it's a complex question and it has legal connotations, it has a legal aspect, but we never know. We are discussing the Territorial Defence in Vukovar. If I've understood things correctly, I was looking at the map this morning and Vukovar is in Croatia, and we have Serbia on the other side, because the river marks the border in a certain sense and we have seen a map of this area. So if Croatia is on one side and we have Vukovar then on the other side and we have Serbia, the Vukovar Territorial Defence represents what exactly? Is it the Territorial Defence of Croatian Vukovar or is it the Territorial Defence of Vukovar but the Serbian Territorial Defence of Vukovar? Because at the time the former Yugoslavia still existed and you seem to be confirming this when you say that the tanks had Yugoslav flags on them. So could you clarify this matter that concerns the Territorial Defence? If not, it's not that important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Territorial Defence was the term that was used, and it was what they called themselves. Now, as far as that Territorial Defence, it had some other, how shall I put this, deeper roots, its source who compiled the Territorial Defence, who was part of it. So do you want me to go into that whole question? I don't know. Anyway, the Territorial Defence is what they called themselves, so that's why we used the term in order to make a better distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to clarify something. Page 87, lines 8 and 9, I'm wondering whether the Chetniks had the same appearance in the uniforms as JNA soldiers. In the English version I can't see this reference to the uniforms. I wanted to mention that. I'd now like to show the witness a document that has to do with a lengthy discussion that he had with Mr. Seselj about an elderly gentleman with a walking stick. I have some copies for the Defence, for the Chamber, and for the witness. This is a document in B/C/S. I don't have the translation yet, but we should be receiving the interpreter's interpretation. Could we put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is the document relevant? Where is it from, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document was found on an Internet site. You can see the reference on the top of the document. It's from the New Agency for Croatia, and the date is 20th of February, 2008.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you forbade me to use newspaper articles, whereas you're allowing the Prosecutor to do -- use Internet articles, and I assume that the newspaper articles are more reliable because you know who the editor is rather than something put on the Internet and you can't get at the source at all. And here I recognise such an amazing piece of stupidity that on this photograph we can see Captain Radic, whereas on the photograph there's no Captain Radic. You see the kind of dupes that are being presented here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as two measures are concerned, I'd like to remind you that the Chamber didn't allow you to use a document, a press article, because the names of incriminated Croats were mentioned in the article and the Chamber decided by majority not to allow you to use this newspaper article. However, we did point out that you would be able to use it through your own witnesses when the time came for that. That's what we decided and we would like to remind you of that. The Chamber doesn't want to prevent you from doing anything, but whenever we have a document we have to check whether it's a relevant document - that's the first thing - and secondly we have to check to see whether the document is prejudicial to certain individuals, individuals who might be called to testify, and then thirdly we have to see whether the document has probative value of any kind. In the document that I have before me today, well, there is a photograph of someone - I don't know who this is, but the Prosecution will perhaps tell us - but as far as relevance is concerned, yes, there is relevance because we have the photograph of someone that we saw in another photograph. It's taken from a different angle, but we can recognise the gentleman with the walking stick. We can recognise the gentleman with the cap and there are other soldiers there and there's another individual. This is a well-known photograph. I don't know why the Prosecution wants to use this photograph, but we have to listen to the question he is going to put.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could the witness first read through this document. It's a fairly short document. And then I will put my question to the witness. Could he read it out slowly so that the interpreters can interpret?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a problem. I, first of all, wanted to say that as far as the preceding decision is concerned, my problem is that -- well, my problem is the link to the witness and the question of relevance, and I have the same problem here. So before we have the witness read out the document, I would like the Prosecution to explain what relevance this document has and in what way this document concerns the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Judge Lattanzi, this article concerns the gentleman we can see with the walking stick. It concerns what happened to him. We have his name that appears in the document. We can see what happened to him. And it has to do with consequences for another person in the photograph. Legally speaking, this person had to answer for his acts, and it's possible with regard to the witness that the witness was familiar with the trial that resulted in this article in the New Agency, so I would like to have him some questions about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood this correctly, well, the Chamber is concerned with the issue of links. And the gentleman with the walking stick, well, Mr. Seselj told us a while ago that this gentleman must have been in a basement. He came out of the basement and he was then escorted somewhere so that he could be taken care of, or something like that. That's Mr. Seselj's version. And on that basis -- well, you say that that is false because the document says the opposite. That's how I have understood the matter. Yes, do answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not want to testify myself and tell you what is true or false. We have a newspaper article that has to do with legal proceedings conducted after what had happened to this gentleman with the walking stick. And as a result of what happened to this gentleman with the walking stick, one of the individuals in the photograph was prosecuted. There was a public trial and I would like to know what the witness knows about this, because he was interviewed at length -- he was questioned at length by Mr. Seselj about this matter and I believe that this is a good base, or this provides good grounds to return to this issue with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If I am not mistaken, I think this photo was first shown in order to elicit from the witness his recognition of various agents in the conflict, notably the issue of the gentleman with the fur bonnet and the insignia and the cockade, in that bonnet, and the also the possible sign on the top of the two helmets of the gentlemen who were waring helmets. The issue of the old man was really a completely non-relevant issue, and if your exhibit here is now to pursue that story, I think it's completely irrelevant. So I would join Judge Lattanzi in saying that this is not relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to clarify something. Mr. Seselj made a certain number of claims about the person in the centre of the photograph. It's important for what happened in Vukovar in general and I'm just going back to allegations made by Mr. Seselj himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber will deliberate to see whether we will authorise you or allow you to use this document or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber has discussed the matter and we will not allow the Prosecution to use the document, given that we believe that it is not relevant in relation to the original use of the photograph which had to do with the cockade caps. Could the Prosecution please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I don't know whether the witness has read the document in the meantime. If he has, maybe I'll ask him some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't ask him any questions about the person with the walking stick.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll move on to something completely different, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Karlovic, you said that in this room in Modateks there were about 20 Chetniks, and then there were some individuals who came to save you from the situation you were in. Could you tell us, can you claim for certainty what their real reasons were, apart from what they said, but what were their real reasons for coming to save you?

utterances.speaker: VILLEM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply I think that that's what those people were like. That was their character. They didn't allow massacres and torture and killing. That's the kind of people they were. And I know that Mare said he that he was a Serb who believed in God, so that's it. I can't go into any deeper motivation or reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. What direct personal knowledge do you have about what they had done previously or prior to the period you had contact with them and after the period you had contact with them, after they had got you out of that house?

utterances.speaker: VILLEM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have that knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. You said after you left the house you were taken to Velepromet; you were treated there. You said that you had been tortured and beaten. Given the physical state you were in, could you see on the faces of these two individuals who had saved you whether they had been involved in reprehensible acts before? Were you in a position to make such observations?

utterances.speaker: VILLEM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have an opportunity to see that, nor could I know what they were doing before.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to notice that the Prosecution here is conducting the cross-examination now and trying to challenge his own witness, it seems. Well, that's something I noticed and you do with it what you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the course of your re-examination -- well, first of all, you should establish a basis, you should remind the witness of the question put to him by the accused, and then you can go back to the answer provided to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to save time, but as far as I can remember the accused asked whether there appeared to be individuals who had been involved in certain acts the day before and then did acts of a different nature later on. I don't have the transcript before me. I was trying to be brief, but it did have a relation to a question put by the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please put your question to the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think he has answered the question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: The accused asked you whether these individuals might have appeared as individuals who had perhaps committed reprehensible acts the day before and then saved you subsequently. So my question is whether your physical condition was such that you were capable of forming an opinion about such a matter.

utterances.speaker: VILLEM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: I made my assessment. In view of their character and how they saved me, I do believe that they weren't people who could kill in cold blood. That's my opinion. But I could not recognise who they belonged to, what they did, what unit they belonged to. I wasn't able to recognise or notice that. So it is my opinion that since they saved me, saved my life, I'm wondering whether they were people who could have committed murders in cold blood. I hope I've made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: That's clear. When you were in the hospital, then the barracks, the JNA barracks, and then Ovcara, did you see or hear Chetniks or other soldiers who were present and did you see them recognising some of the prisoners as prisoners who had been at the front line, some of the prisoners as having participated in combat? Did they identify any prisoners in this way?

utterances.speaker: VILLEM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that could be noticed most at Ovcara. There was that at Ovcara. Now, as to the hospital, I can't remember. As to the barracks, I don't remember. I know that people were recognised at Ovcara mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I understand. And one last matter that I would like to clarify. The accused showed you a number of documents that concerned an interview with the military security service, and there was a quote from a transcript from the Mrksic case, and you talked about contact two days before you came to testify at the Tribunal. I wasn't sure I understood this correctly. I wanted to clarify the matter because the quote was out of context. So what I would like to know is the following: When you said, "Yes, we had contact two days before I came to testify here," when you said that, were you referring to your testimony in 1996 or were you referring to your testimony before the Tribunal in 2006?

utterances.speaker: VILLEM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I might be allowed to put you right on one point so that we can understand this, the document was mostly written in general terms. Perhaps I was wrong, but I didn't see that it was strictly stated anywhere that two days before the arrival to the Mrksic case I was prepared or proofed. So can we take a look at that again, but I don't think that I saw that anywhere, that Vilim Karlovic was proofed two days before arriving to take part in those proceedings. They are general documents where the service gave its reports, and between 1996 to 1998, sometime during that period, that's when it was. And I never ever had any conversations with anybody from the Croatian Intelligence Services after that, and nobody except my family in fact knows that I am here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: In any event, this occurred on one occasion and only in 1996? That is what I want to find out.

utterances.speaker: VILLEM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, because I have no reason why I wouldn't say it if it happened again. If it did, I would have said. But it didn't, so no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no other questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if none of the Judges has any questions for the witness, I would like to thank the witness for having come to testify in The Hague and I wish you a safe trip home. I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to all of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm addressing the Prosecution now. Is the following witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes. The Prosecution calls Dragutin Berghofer, and my colleague, Mr. Ferrara, will be leading this witness pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber would like to greet Mr. Ferrara, who is appearing for the first time before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the first time. I joined the Office of the Prosecutor in October 2007, and it's first time for me before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to remind you that we said that the Prosecution would have 30 minutes at its disposal for this witness, and Mr. Seselj will have an hour and a half for his cross-examination, if he wishes to cross-examine the witness. Mr. Ferrara, according to the 92 ter procedure, you have to give us a brief summary of the written statement, once the witness is in the courtroom. We need to have the witness in the courtroom. A minute ago I was told that he had disappeared. I hope that we have found him now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Yes, we found him later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The usher says no. [In English] The witness, no? [Interpretation] The witness has disappeared yet again. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was informed about 20 minutes ago that the witness was on his way here. So I'm not sure which hotel he's staying in and how long it will take him to get here. We can either take a brief adjournment, or we can simply call the witness tomorrow morning. We're at the disposal of the Chamber. And of course perhaps Mr. Registrar has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the latest information, he is in the building and on his way. But we must still make sure that he comes to the right courtroom. I take advantage to check with Mr. Seselj and for him to confirm that he still does not wish to cross-examine this witness. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will never agree to cross-examine any witness under 92 ter, bis, and quater, and no witness who is testifying via videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If there is nothing further on that point, perhaps while we're waiting for the witness to arrive, I could take this opportunity to raise one other issue if I might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 7th of March, 2008, the Prosecution filed a motion to return 10 exhibits to the 65 ter list. That filing contained a confidential annex listing these documents. The second document in that table, the B/C/S version bearing ERN 0094-9847-0094-9852, already appears on the current 65 ter list as number 1523. Upon reviewing this filing, it appears that the same document was on our previous exhibit list twice, the old numbers being 1585 and 1339, and that the 65 ter number -- the old 65 ter number 1595 that appeared in the first Rule 94(B) motion was deleted as a duplicate from the recapitulated list of exhibits. Current 65 ter number 1523, bearing the exhibit -- the ERN number that I just mentioned, does not need to be added to the current exhibit list. Nevertheless, the Prosecution requests the Chamber to consider this document with the 94(B) motion that was filed earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have taken note of this and the Chamber will render a decision after having heard the observations of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, in the French translation the number that you referred to, the 65 ter number that you referred to in line 1 on page 101 came out as 1923, so I just want to ensure that what is now in the transcript is the correct number. It says 1523.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Harhoff. It is indeed -- the numbers as appearing on the English transcript are in fact correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Let me check first that you can hear the translation of what I'm saying in your own language. Could you please give me your first and last name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dragutin Berghofer. Date of birth, 29th of October, 1940, born in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a profession or an occupation or are you retired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified in a court of law about the events that took place in ex-Yugoslavia, and if so in which court of law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have, Your Honour. This is my fourth time to come here. I have testified three times previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. You have already testified three times. If you recall, can you tell me in which cases you testified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the first time it was for Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic, that was twice in that case, and once for Mr. Seselj -- no, sorry, Mr. Sljivancanin. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And on the three occasions that you came, was it at the request of the Prosecution? Were you a witness for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Will you please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you sir, you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few brief explanations from me. As this is the fourth time you are, you know how we function but perhaps not within the framework of this particular proceeding under 92 ter. You will be answering a few brief questions put to you by Mr. Ferrara, whom you have met, and for this we envisage a half an hour. At the end of this period it would be normal for the accused to cross-examine you, but he has told us that he will not cross-examine you. Possibly the Judges who are in front of you may be asking you questions. So I now give the floor to Mr. Ferrara, who is going to first of all make a brief summary of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness lived in Dragutin Berghofer Vukovar since he was six years old and until the day of the fall of the town in November 1991. He was a businessman --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apologies. We cannot interpret at this speed, thank you, and we don't have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I have only paper text but I can provide ... He was an entrepreneur. He owned five shops and many houses in Vukovar. He was divorced with two daughters. Vesna was 17 years old and Jasna was 26 years old at the time, and he was living with a woman called Ljubica. On the 24th of August, 1991, the war in Vukovar burst out and in three months he lost everything. The same day the war started, his house was destroyed, shot by a JNA tank, and he was forced to live in a basement with more than 40 people until the takeover of the town. On the 15th of September, 1991, his daughter Vesna was taken away to Negoslavci by soldiers of the JNA who were cleaning the area. Eventually discovered that after the fall of Vukovar, she was brought back to her home, but around the 10th of December, 1991, his daughter was taken away again by some locals who turned her to the Serbian side. And in 2000 or 2001, her body was discovered in the Vukovar cemetery. On the 6th of November, 1991, his partner Ljubica was killed during a shelling when a piece of shrapnel hit her in the neck. When the war started Mr. Berghofer joined the Vukovar defence, and in fact he was later recognised as a member of the ZNG. He was not a combatant, but he was in charge of food, supplies, and logistics, for the people who lived in the basement in the town. On 17th November, 1991, Mr. Berghofer led a column of more than 300 people for a breakthrough, but soon he realised that it was impossible to leave the town due to heavy shelling by the JNA and the minefields set up around the city, so he decided to come back to the hospital. Meanwhile, the people that were capable of walking had gone to the hospital, as the Serb forces told them on loudspeakers, that if they gone there they could wait for the convoy to take them to Zagreb -- to Zagreb. He found the situation of total chaos at the hospital. People were crying in the corridors and the wounded were up to three in a bed. He stayed there three nights and he fed himself with milk powder for babies. At about 4 p.m. on 19th November, 1991, reserve soldiers and members of the JNA entered the compound and the hospital premises. During the same time Mr. Berghofer -- during the same night, sorry, Mr. Berghofer heard the sound of 18 gunshots being fired and the sound of buses and trucks which started the evacuation of the hospital. The morning of the 19th of November, 1991, the witness with other people was searched, boarded in a bus, and taken to the JNA barracks. The detainees were made to stay on the bus for about four hours, and all around people dressed with different kind of uniform and in civilian clothes, with long beards and unkempt, walked around the bus celebrating their victory, screaming, cursing, insulting, and threatening the detainees, and also showing them weapons, such as long rifles and knives. More than 15 people were taken off by the bus, kicked, and beaten ferociously and loaded into military buses and driven off towards Negoslavci. Later when the witness found them -- found these people at Ovcara, their heads were all swollen up and they were entirely covered in blood. At about 1 p.m. on the 20th of November, the bus left the barracks toward Ovcara Farm. There the detainees were searched again, stripped off their belongings, and forced to enter the hangar to a gauntlet formed by a number of armed Serbian men wearing different types of uniforms and civilian clothes who beat and kicked severely them with everything they had - iron bar, rifles, large pieces of wood, fists, kicks. There the witness saw that Milos Bulic, known as Bulidza, beat Damjan Samardzic, nicknamed the "Big Boiler," with a baseball bat, and afterwards he did not show any sign of life. He saw also that Gaspar FNU and another man were beaten to death upon arrival at the hangar. Inside the hangar the witness saw a miserable atmosphere, with people screaming, beatings, yelling, trampling on people, hitting them with iron rods, and rifle butts. In the middle of the hangar there were a mix of straw and blood. Inside the hangar he saw the reporter, Sinisa Glavasevic, beaten to death and another man, Vladimir Djukic, brutally beaten with his very own crutch. Later the witness was separated with other people, put into a small van to be taken to Velepromet, where there was no space. So he was brought to Modateks factory where he spent the night. There he was beaten, assaulted and interrogated. The next morning he was brought to Velepromet where he entered the so-called "Room of Death" and there he saw a lot of his acquaintances beaten and taken away. Rene Matausek, the son of Dzemo, Crk, Golac, and Tihomir Perkovic. Mr. Berghofer hasn't seen them again. He was saved by a JNA captain who took him to the JNA barracks just before midnight on the 21st of November. Later he was imprisoned for four and a half months at Sremska Mitrovica, and on the 27th of March 1992 he was exchanged. That would conclude the summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Before we discuss the exhibits, Mr. Berghofer, did you meet with a representative of the OTP on March, 6 March, 2008?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you provide a statement to those representatives about what happened to you and other people in 1991 in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review your written statement in your language?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Which is your language?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Registrar, if we can call up for -- the document 65 ter number 7178. Sorry, Your Honour, the number is 7183. It's the 92 statement of the witness Dragutin Berghofer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Witness, looking at the first page, does the first page bear your signature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: And if you could flip through those other pages, do those other pages, at the bottom, bear your initials?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I can't see them. I only see it where the list of victims from Ovcara are. No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Ms. Usher, if you can show.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those are initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Yes. So do you recognise your initials at the bottom of the pages?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, yes, I recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Does this document reflect the date on which you signed it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes. It was on the 6th of this month.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Does this statement accurately reflect your recollection of the events described herein?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I proceed? Here and there, there may be one or two words that could be slightly changed to the left or the right, but otherwise everything is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would move for the admission of this document, 65 ter number 7183, into exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can we have an exhibit number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P278, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Registrar, can you call up the 65 ter number 7178, should be -- there's some problem ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. Witness, you said at a certain point when the Prosecutor asked you whether the document is in conformity with what you said, you said yes, but a word here or there could be more to the left or to the right. What is the word that you would have liked changed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as I understand, Your Honour, my daughter was 17, but one daughter was 27 and the other was 26. And then my wedded wife, the mother of these two daughters, was Jelka Djitko, and Ljubica was a friend, but one could call her an unmarried wife or a partner. Could I add something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have quickly reached Velepromet. We didn't refer to Modateks because certain things happened there, too. Those would be my comments. But in my statement I will come back to that, in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you well, the one who was killed on the 6th of November is your concubine, your mistress, not your wife, the one you married and whom you divorced in 1982? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. We can call her a friend or an unwed -- a common-law wife.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can we call up the document 65 ter number 2513.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer --

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: -- do you recognise this photo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What's it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: That is the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How many nights did you spend there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, from the 17th, the night of the 17th, the 18th, up until the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Where were you taken away from the hospital? And where?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: We went first to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to move for the admission of this document into exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar, can we have an exhibit number for this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P279, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Registrar, can you call up 65 ter number 4040, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Berghofer, could you describe for the Court what the photo represents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That is the road leading to Negoslavci and that is the side entrance to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: You should have an electronic pen. Could you mark the direction the bus entered the compound, the JNA barracks. Is this from outside that we see the barracks or from inside?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: From the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: From inside.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the compound, into the buses?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, let us say, Your Honours, from 8.30 or 9.00 we were still in the hospital, then you add 15 minutes and then four or five hours, because we reached Ovcara at exactly 1.30. I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you describe us very quickly what's happened when you were in the buses, what's happened outside the buses?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I can, Judge. We arrived in six buses with Zrenjanin registration plates. The buses had about 45 seats each, and for about four hours, maybe a little longer, we sat there. During that time we were guarded by young soldiers at the doors of the buses and for -- then Professor Licina got off my bus; a watch-maker, Hedik; and Nurse Biba's husband -- I beg your pardon. Just now I can't remember the name, but I will remember. Three persons got off and they were set free. Then they pulled out some others from some other buses. So I thought, They are lucky; somebody must have taken them off. However, when I saw that they were being kicked around and hit on the head with rifle butts, pushed with their hands and beaten, I changed my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: This happened in the compound where you marking before?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. All those who were taken off the bus, at least those I saw being kicked, they were put on a seventh military bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you mark in the photo where that's happening?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: It's narrow. There were other buildings here in the compound, within the barracks compound, and we were standing away from this -- from where this photograph is taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender into exhibit 65 ter number 4040, page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit P280.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I add, the third person was Koljesar. Nurse Biba's husband, Koljesar, he worked in Elektro Slavonija. That is the third person.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, where were you taken after the barracks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: We were taken to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Registrar, I would like to call up 65 ter number 2825.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, I wish to tell you that you have another five minutes left of the time attributed to you, so if the Judges have no questions to put to the witness, we could finish today.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I have some few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, what's this list?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: This is a list of all the boys I found in Ovcara and with whom I was beaten, together with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Who wrote this list?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: It must be about two years ago. I had 10 minutes available to me and I made up this list on the spot, offhand.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Where did you see the people indicated in this list?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: They were with me at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Have you ever seen these people again?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do you know if they were found later, and where?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Some were found at Ovcara and some have still not been found, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When you say -- when you say "Some were found at Ovcara," what do you mean? Were they found alive or dead?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Dead. Dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: You said that you wrote this list about two years ago. Where exactly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: When the Prosecutor was Mr. Moore, here. I think it was on the 3rd of March, 2006. There's a date on top.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So did you write the list before testifying in some trial?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I had another list before this. Ever since 1992 when I left Mitrovica, I had a piece of paper and I wrote down all the names I could remember as soon as I returned from prison. However, I didn't bring it with me when talking to Mr. Moore. So he didn't force me, but he simply said how come I didn't bring it. But I never carried it with me. And then within 10 minutes I wrote it down, what I could remember. These were sons of my colleagues. Some were my friends. Some people are of the same age of me, people I grew up with. So there was no problem for me to compile this name -- this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender into exhibit the document 65 ter number 2825. Just last question. Please, Mr. Registrar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P281, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Registrar, can you call up 65 ter number 4103.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, can you describe to the Court what the photo represents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: This is a picture of Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you mark with the pen the entrance of the Velepromet and the room where you were taken?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: This was known as the "Room of Death."

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: You can mark it with a cross if you want, also with a big cross.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Is this the entrance?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: To the right. This is also the road leading to Negoslavci. Up there is the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Where you put an arrow, what's there? You made two marks, one on the right and one on the left.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What's there on the left?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: On the left is the so-called "Room of Death." That is where we were placed when we got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Why the room was called the "Room of Death"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Because, Your Honours, apart from seven or eight of us, no others came out alive. No others returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you put number 1 next to the "Room of Death"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember the names of the people who were taken away from the room when you were -- when you were there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Very well, because I knew them. I'm a local of Vukovar, and already in 1992, 1993, I told these names. There was Matausek, Golac, Tihomir Perkovic. Among the Gypsies, Dzema, the accordion player's son; Crk, who was manager of Pik, a plant, a slaughterhouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Have you ever seen them again?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do you know if they were found or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Tihomir Perkovic, with whom I was saved at Ovcara, as far as I know he was never found.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Any other?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I think, as far as I know, Matausek was not found either. As for Golac, his father was in Germany. He looked for him there and I never again heard of him or his father. Actually, they were not found.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, were all these people you mentioned civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: As far as I know among the persons, only the son of the Gypsy Dzema was in uniform. He was short, about 1 metre 60. This man lifted him up, put him on the table, this reservist, the same person who took them all out later on, and he said, "This is a real Zenga and not you," using the word for women's genitals, and he used the actual word itself, referring to the rest of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: The last question: You statement you say repeatedly "Chetniks." What do you mean for "Chetniks"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, you see, as I grew up in Yugoslavia and I watched the partisan films, the Chetniks were shown wearing cockades, with beards, carrying knives, like killers. That's how they were portrayed in films. However, what happened now was that some of them still wore this so-called Serb sajkaca, they wore insignia, and they had beards.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you see these kind of people in Vukovar during the war, dressed as you described now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender into exhibit the document 65 ter number 4103.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P282, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I want to enter all the above-mentioned documents that are attached to the 92 ter statement that we tender into an exhibit at the beginning of the interview. I don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have just one question before closing, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How do you make a distinction between the Chetniks and JNA soldiers or members of the Territorial Defence? On what basis do you make that distinction.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it was like this: Soldiers of the regular army wore olive-grey uniforms. The local reservists wore older JNA uniforms. Some local people of Vukovar were in civilian clothes and some were people we had never seen before. Like Topala, the sniper, for instance, he wore the Montenegrin cap. Then some people in the barracks wore sajkacas, and in Ovcara also they wore these sajkacas, or traditional caps with certain insignia, so that I assessed them to be Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, your testimony has now been completed, as the accused will not be cross-examining you. Thank you for coming at the request of the Prosecution and the Chamber conveys its sympathy to you for everything that happened to your family, your daughter, and your partner. I would now like to ask Madam Usher to be kind enough to accompany you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will very quickly discuss with the Prosecution the programme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tomorrow we could have heard the witness envisaged for next week. That will not be possible, Mr. Mundis, the witness planned?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, that witness does not arrive until Sunday here in The Hague, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then we will find ourselves in the same situation as today, because Mr. Seselj will not cross-examine so we will be proceeding very quickly with the witness planned for Tuesday. So could you also prepare with the following witness planned for Wednesday and Thursday so that as of Tuesday we can begin with the following witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We will endeavour to do that, Mr. President. I will also indicate at this point in time and follow up as soon as we're able to do so that we are undertaking also a review of videotapes with an eye towards perhaps showing videotapes as a means of ensuring that the courtroom is fully utilised. Once we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tomorrow we can have used the time available for the videos?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We very well could be in a position. Perhaps if I was, this afternoon, to consult with members of my team, we could provide to the Chamber and to Dr. Seselj a list of videos perhaps to be shown as early as tomorrow. Perhaps if I could be given a couple of hours in order to make a determination on that and we could notify the Chamber by way of the legal officer and Dr. Seselj by way of the Detention Unit exactly which videos we would be in a position to show tomorrow so everyone is fully aware of what we will be doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, last time you told us that you are not opposed regarding the videos. Do you still take that position?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that is not quite what I said. I said that it is possible for videotapes to be admitted directly into evidence without hearing a certain witness, going with a witness, but only on condition that I am shown on those videotapes engaged in any kind of activity. Only then can those videotapes be admitted into evidence directly. In all other cases videotapes have to be explained, their origin has to be established, their relevance, and everything else. And how do you imagine that I get a list of videotapes this evening and for them to be shown tomorrow already?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the video list is something that you have had for a long time. You have all those videos and you have probably viewed them. The interest in everyone seeing those videos is to -- for all of us to see them, and then if necessary those videos can be shown again when we have witnesses. For example, the video we saw this morning, if it was already shown before, everybody would have seen it and the Prosecutor could have shown the video again. So this would allow us to save time. My understanding was that you were in agreement for the videos, but you are not in agreement on the other videos where -- that don't show you, and I think that you maintain that position now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, four or five years ago I received videotapes with a total duration of over 100 hours. That is in 2003 and 2004, when they were sending me these classical videotapes, until they started sending me DVDs. When they started with the DVDs, I refused to see them. So videotapes shown on a video player were of a duration of more than a hundred hours. That's quite certain. There's all kinds of things there on those tapes. If I were to assess the relevance, maybe not more than 5 per cent of them are relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, in view of the objections, it is already a bit too late because between now and tomorrow it's not possible to deal with the matter. You have to send us a list of videotapes that you might show us and then Mr. Seselj will make his comments and then the Chamber will decide, because otherwise it would be going too fast to show videos tomorrow because there may be problems. So the best idea is to draw up a list of videotapes. There are three categories. The first category are videotapes showing Mr. Seselj making speeches, the second category of videotapes which are CNN, SkyNews, or who knows who's stories about certain events, and then a third category could be videos which necessarily need to be produced through a witness. So please make a list of these different categories, and then Mr. Seselj will say, I agree, I don't agree, and then we will be able to show those videos. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It will be done, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, tomorrow we will not be having any hearings. We will resume next Tuesday, at 2.15, because we are working in the afternoons. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I request, Mr. President, for the four hours lost tomorrow to be discounted from the available time for the Prosecution, because it is their fault that they don't have a witness ready tomorrow. These are four hours that we are losing. That's another problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, do you wish to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It's my understanding that the time that the Prosecution has been allocated consists of direct examination time and consequently if there is no direct examination, there is no time to be allocated to the Prosecution. I would also place on the record at this point in time that although I understand now, and it is clear now, that Dr. Seselj will not cross any of the 92 ter witnesses, at the time the calendars are produced and the witnesses are scheduled, it was completely unclear to us whether in fact he would cross-examine witnesses or not. Producing witnesses, as the Trial Chamber is well aware, is not something that can be done in 24 hours. Visas are required. It generally takes five working days to process and get witnesses here, so that our lead time is five to 10 days down the road in terms of getting witnesses here. So we simply can't stop on a dime, as they say, and produce witnesses, nor can the schedule be altered in a quick manner. So we would oppose what Dr. Seselj has suggested for the reasons that I've just indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as early as last year I cautioned that I would not cross the 92 ter witnesses, and you will remember that. You were the Pre-Trial Judge in those days. I fought for a year emphatically against the implementation of those rules in these proceedings, so what I said was not a surprise. Maybe you didn't believe me, that I really would refuse to cross-examine them, but that's another problem. Frequently people are mistaken because they don't believe me in due time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Concerning the time, the time allocated to the Prosecution by the Chamber is a time which was a function of the written statements and the intentions of the Prosecution. Regarding the witness for which 30 minutes was given, those 30 minutes were used. However, the time for the cross-examination, if he doesn't use it, it's too bad for him, so it is time that is lost and which could not be made up for. Having said that, it is not 2.15 Tuesday but 2.45. I have to make myself clear. Thank you, and we will meet on Tuesday, at 2.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 18th day of March, 2008, at 2.45 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.34 p.m.,
